title: What DeployCo Actually Is
description: A ten billion dollar joint venture, an acquisition that closed in July and a second one that has not, and the Australian team you would be joining. Everything checkable, as of the eighteenth of August.

lines.text: The people who funded this company were promised a seventeen and a half percent annual return.
Not hoped for. Promised, over five years, as reported terms of the joint venture.
Every fund wants that. Wanting it is not the same as being owed it.
Which is why the number matters. A consultancy with a contractual return has a clock on every engagement.
That clock is the thing you will feel on a Tuesday afternoon in a client's office.
So the interesting question is not what they build. It is how fast they have to prove it.
Exactly. And their own website answers it in three words: build, prove, generalise.
This is The DeployCo Screen. Everything in this episode is checkable and dated the eighteenth of August.
Here is the lazy version. It is OpenAI's consulting arm. That is the whole story.
It is not the whole story, and the gap is where your questions on Thursday come from.
DeployCo is a separate company, majority owned by OpenAI, funded by outside investors.
It has bought one consultancy, agreed to buy a second, and is standing up a team in Sydney right now.
Three of those facts post-date the pack you wrote for your application. That is why this episode exists.
Three moving parts. The venture, the acquisitions, and the Australian team.
One, the venture. OpenAI launched the Deployment Company on the eleventh of May this year.
Reported structure: a ten billion dollar vehicle, with OpenAI committing up to one and a half billion.
Five hundred million at close, with an option for a further billion. Nineteen investors in total.
TPG anchors it, alongside Brookfield, Advent International, Bain Capital and Goanna Capital.
Private equity money in an AI services business. That is a bet on billable hours, not on models.
It is a bet on deployment being the bottleneck. Their own framing says the models are not the constraint any more.
Two, the acquisitions. Tomoro was the founding one, announced in May and formally done on the first of July.
The UK register shows what that meant. On that day all eight Tomoro directors resigned together.
They were replaced by a single OpenAI-side director based in San Francisco.
So the founders are gone and it is an OpenAI shell now.
No. That is corporate governance, not an exodus. The founders still publish and still speak at conferences.
Tomoro was founded in twenty twenty-three in alliance with OpenAI. It brought roughly a hundred and fifty forward deployed engineers.
Then on the eighth of July they announced a second one. A company called Northslope.
Never heard of them.
Neither had most people. Northslope was the first member of Palantir's Vanguard Elite network.
Its revenue grew seven times in twenty twenty-five, with customers across the United States, Europe and the Middle East.
Cancer detection in healthcare, supply chain bottlenecks in manufacturing, renewable megawatts on the grid.
That deal has not closed. It is still subject to regulatory approval, and the two companies remain separate until it does.
Then why does it matter to a Sydney candidate at all?
Because of one sentence in the announcement. After closing, Northslope may support joint commercial engagements with Palantir.
One caveat before you use that on Thursday. Northslope has offices in New York, London and Denver.
None in this region. So it cannot mean more people in Sydney. Say it that way and you sound accurate.
A forward deployed engineering firm partnering with the original forward deployed engineering firm. That changes what the work looks like.
Three, Australia. Tomoro launched here in December twenty twenty-five, in Sydney and Melbourne.
It is led by Dan Edgar, formerly Accenture's banking data and AI lead, with KPMG and Deloitte before that.
The stated target was forty to fifty staff within twelve months.
Now what an engagement actually looks like, in their own published examples.
Their definition: forward deployed engineering teams work directly with customers to solve a specific problem.
Then validate the impact, then identify the patterns that scale. Build, prove, generalise.
Two case studies are on the front page. BBVA, the bank, and John Deere, the tractor company.
BBVA started with ChatGPT Enterprise and is now scaling to a hundred and twenty thousand employees across twenty-five countries.
John Deere is the more useful one for you. Read how they describe it.
They reviewed hundreds of real-world examples with domain experts. They built custom evaluation systems to measure accuracy.
Then they iterated to improve model performance. The result was seventy percent less chemical usage for farmers.
So the headline number is the chemical reduction. That is what a client buys.
The headline number is what a client buys. The evaluation system is what made anyone believe the number.
That sentence is the argument you have been making at work for four months. It is on their front page.
There is one public engagement in this region. CapitaLand, in Singapore.
Seven AI Experience Days, more than a hundred and twenty employees, over a hundred use cases, fifty prototypes.
Built with Codex, described in a CapitaLand post that Isabelle herself reshared.
And the Australian clients?
Not public. The launch coverage said only a major airline and a major telco in this region.
Do not guess at names on Thursday. Guessing wrong in front of a recruiter is unrecoverable.
One more thing about how they work, from their own head of talent, in numbers.
Thirty people at the start of twenty twenty-five. About a hundred and fifty now.
Four hundred applications running in the cloud, and twelve weeks on average from proof of concept to production.
Teams of three to six. Engineers work on one project at a time.
One project at a time is not how consultancies work. That is how product teams work.
Which is the point, and it is worth saying back to her. It is the opposite of the timesheet world.
The numbers, said twice, because you cannot glance back at audio.
Eleventh of May: the venture launches. First of July: Tomoro formally becomes DeployCo.
Eighth of July: the Northslope announcement, still unclosed. Seventh of August: the Sydney role goes live.
Ten billion dollar vehicle. Nineteen investors. Roughly a hundred and fifty engineers from Tomoro.
More than two million businesses now use OpenAI, double a year ago. Codex has over five million weekly users.
Those last two are marketing figures in an acquisition announcement.
They are, and you should treat them that way. They are context, not evidence.
Eleven roles are open on their board today, across New York, San Francisco, London, Edinburgh, Paris, Sydney and Melbourne.
Sydney and Melbourne went live last, on the seventh of August, a month after London and Paris.
Australia was opened last, which tells you the Australian pod is being stood up right now.
Knowing all of this is a liability if you use it badly. Three ways it backfires.
First: reciting it. You list the investors, the valuation and the acquisition dates at a recruiter.
That shows preparation. Why is that bad?
Because none of it is about the job, and she has heard it from every candidate this month.
Preparation reads as insight only when it changes a question you ask. Otherwise it reads as revision.
Second: getting a detail wrong with confidence. Say the Northslope deal has closed and you have taught her to check you.
It has not closed. It is pending regulatory approval. Say agreed to acquire, not acquired.
Third: naming a client you cannot source. The Australian accounts are not public and one commonly repeated name is unverified.
The early signal for all three is the same. If a fact is not attached to a question, do not say it.
Two facts and one question. That is the whole homework budget for a thirty minute call.
Fact one: build, prove, generalise. Their words for the cycle you have been arguing for.
Fact two: John Deere shipped behind a custom evaluation system. Their words for shadow mode.
The question: what does Northslope mean for the Australian team? Nobody outside can answer it, so it is a real question.
And if she does not know?
Then you have learned something useful, and she will remember being asked something she had to think about.
Self-test. Has the Northslope acquisition closed, and what is the one word that makes the difference?
The word is agreed. They have agreed to acquire, and it is still pending approval.
Next time: the first ninety seconds. The answer that decides how the other twenty-eight minutes go.
